If a pair of crossings can appear together, the count must know whether they cancel; if a cell is subdivided, the count must know which new pieces offset each other.
contract.evidence: The protected evidence is the total that legal redrawings cannot change, even though individual local events may appear or disappear. The total remembers forced structure rather than clutter because the harmless changes have already been audited one local move at a time.
contract.output: The output is a number, sign total, or parity fact that can prove impossibility, force existence, or compare two legally related pictures. One honest computation then applies across all legal versions because the count has already shown it survives the permitted changes.
contract.failure_test: Reject the argument if the count changes under a legal harmless move, if signs are assigned without a shared rule, or if the count is taken before the object and allowed changes are named. A count earns trust only by surviving the allowed changes.

families.title: Surface bookkeeping
families.purpose: Connect small patches, boundary behavior, holes, handles, side choices, and gluing rules to conclusions that belong to the completed surface rather than one local drawing.
families.first_principles: This family treats a surface as a connected ledger. Local behavior can be drawn patch by patch, but the patches must agree when glued back together. The whole surface may force a count, side reversal, boundary term, or defect that no single patch reveals by itself.

depth.human_problem: The human problem is that surfaces look simple nearby but can behave differently as wholes. This family asks how patches, boundaries, holes, handles, gluing rules, and orientation combine into whole-surface facts that local inspection alone misses completely. It teaches why a small ordinary-looking neighborhood is not the whole story.
depth.first_principles: Cut the surface into manageable pieces, understand what happens on each piece, and then glue the bookkeeping back together. The global result is not guessed from one patch; it is forced by how all patches fit, how edges match, and whether local choices can survive a full trip around the surface.
depth.how_it_works: Surface bookkeeping uses decompositions, orientation choices, boundary terms, and cancellation. It is careful about what is local and what is global, because many surface obstructions appear only after a full trip around the object or a full sum over its pieces. The proof asks what the completed surface permits all local accounts to do together.
depth.course_examples: The Mobius strip reveals global one-sidedness. Surface classification tracks handles and crosscaps. Euler characteristic records whole-surface type. Poincare-Hopf shows that vector fields must obey the surface's total count. The same surface facts keep reappearing in different language, from paper-strip travel to the final question of whether arrows can agree everywhere.
depth.failure_mode: The common failure is to reason locally and assume the whole surface behaves the same way. A Mobius strip defeats that assumption immediately, and later orientation-dependent counts fail without global consistency across the surface. Another failure is counting pieces before reading the gluing rule that tells what surface those pieces actually make.

essay: Surface bookkeeping is needed because a surface can lie to local inspection. Every tiny patch of a sphere, torus, disk, or Mobius strip may look like an ordinary piece of paper. The difference appears when patches are glued into a whole: a route may return reversed, a boundary may add a term, a handle may create a new loop, or a missing disk may change what can be filled.

This family teaches the reader to track the whole surface without losing the local pieces. Divide the surface into manageable parts, count or orient those parts, then check what survives when they are put back together. Euler characteristic, boundary orientation, surface classification, and Poincare-Hopf all depend on this discipline.

From first principles, a surface is both local room and global instruction. Local room lets the course draw curves, arrows, neighborhoods, and small crossings. Global instruction says how those local rooms attach to each other. A sphere, torus, and Mobius band can all look locally ordinary while placing different demands on loops, side choices, and vector fields.

The family connects early strip examples to late dynamics. The Mobius strip shows a local side choice failing after a full trip. Euler characteristic shows a surface count surviving many decompositions. Poincare-Hopf shows the same surface count controlling the total defect of an arrow field. The object has changed, but the bookkeeping habit is the same: local facts must be reconciled with the whole surface.

Local freedom is not the same as global freedom. A patch may allow an arrow, a side choice, or a sign, while the completed surface refuses to let all those local choices agree at once. Surface bookkeeping is how the course finds the refusal.

The pieces support the proof only when the recombination is honest: shared edges must be matched correctly, boundary terms must not vanish by wish, and side choices must be checked after a full trip.
contract.evidence: The protected evidence is the global surface account: Euler characteristic, orientability, boundary behavior, or a total controlled by the surface. This evidence belongs to the whole surface, not one patch, because the whole surface decides whether the local accounts can agree.
contract.output: The output is a whole-surface conclusion that local inspection alone could not justify. It says what every local choice must obey when the surface is completed, such as whether a side choice returns reversed or whether a total count must match the surface.
contract.failure_test: Reject the argument if it assumes every local choice glues globally, ignores boundary terms, counts before applying gluing rules, or changes the surface while keeping the old name. Those errors replace the real surface with an easier one.

families.title: Drawing and embedding arguments
families.purpose: Ask whether required connections, loops, or strands can live in the chosen surrounding space without forbidden crossings, lost over-under data, or illegal pass-through moves.
families.first_principles: This family studies room. A page, sphere, torus, or other surface gives routes and limitations. The answer may be decided before a perfect drawing is found, because the real issue is whether every legal placement faces the same route constraint.

depth.human_problem: The human problem is to know whether one object can sit inside another without forbidden collisions. A drawing may suggest an answer, but this family asks for a reason that covers every drawing and every legal attempt. It replaces drawing frustration with an audit of the object, the room, and the forbidden moves.
depth.first_principles: Separate the object's required connections from the room supplied by the surrounding surface or space. If every legal placement would force a forbidden meeting, the obstruction belongs to the topology, not to a bad drawing. The object and the receiving room must both be named before the placement question is meaningful.
depth.how_it_works: Embedding arguments track crossings, over-under information, winding, linking, endpoint order, and surface room. They ask whether deformation can remove intersections or whether a count proves that some relation survives every allowed placement in the space under study. The proof must explain why the obstruction defeats all legal placements, not just one sketch.
depth.course_examples: Path puzzles in a disk, planar graph questions, knots and links, and intersection theory all belong here. The family teaches the reader to distinguish accidental crossings from forced ones by checking what legal motion can remove. Later, the same habit helps separate a visible meeting from a signed intersection that cannot be dismissed.
depth.failure_mode: The common failure is to confuse a failed attempt with a proof of impossibility. A topological obstruction must show that every legal attempt fails, not only the first drawing tried or the first plausible arrangement. A second failure is forgetting data that the flat drawing hides, such as over-under order or the surface that supplies the routes.

essay: Drawing and embedding arguments ask whether there is enough room for required connections. A failed drawing is not enough, because a better drawing may exist. The family therefore separates the object that must be placed from the space that must receive it. Which endpoints are fixed? Which crossings are forbidden? Can one strand pass through another? Does the surrounding surface have holes or handles that provide alternate routes?

This is where knots, links, planar graphs, path puzzles, and intersection arguments meet. Each problem asks whether a relation can be removed by legal motion or whether it belongs to the shape of the situation. A crossing on the page may be accidental. A linking relation or forced intersection may survive every attempt to redraw.

From first principles, embedding is a room test. The object has demands: these points must connect, this loop must close, these strands may not pass through each other. The surrounding space has allowances: routes around holes, extra dimensions, boundaries, or a flat page with no overpass. The proof asks whether the allowances can satisfy the demands without violating the rules.

This family also teaches the difference between a drawing and an obstruction. A drawing is one attempt. An obstruction is a reason every legal attempt fails. That reason may be boundary order in a disk, linking in space, a signed intersection count, or a shortage of dimensions. The course keeps returning to this distinction because visual failure alone is too weak.

The method is not testing drawing skill. It is proving that all legal drawings face the same constraint. The surface or surrounding space supplies only certain routes, and sometimes those routes are not enough. When that happens, the failure belongs to the topology of the placement problem.

families.title: Motion through possible states
families.purpose: Turn mechanical or physical questions into questions about complete states, legal paths, forbidden regions, fixed points, equilibria, and barriers in the space of all possibilities.
families.first_principles: This family replaces the object in motion with the space of all its possible positions. Holes and walls in that space explain blocked motions, unavoidable coincidences, and forced positions. The translation must record every freedom and every forbidden state, or the topological answer may describe the model instead of the real motion.

depth.human_problem: The human problem is to understand motion when exact equations or trajectories are unavailable. This family asks what the shape of possible states can force before anything is solved second by second or computed point by point. It lets the course reason about behavior by first making the space of possible behavior honest.
depth.first_principles: Represent each complete possible state as a point in a new space. Complete means enough information to recover the situation the question cares about: positions, angles, boundary conditions, contacts, and forbidden collisions. Motion becomes a path or rule on that space. Fixed points, equilibria, blocked routes, and forced passages become questions about the shape of the allowed state space.
depth.how_it_works: The family translates physical or dynamical behavior into shape: graph of a rule against self-agreement, vector-field defects, index sums, or paths in a configuration space. Once translated, earlier tools such as deformation and surviving counts apply, but the translation remains part of the proof. The model must say what one point means and what one path means.
depth.course_examples: The center-of-gravity demonstration, Brouwer fixed point theorem, vector fields, equilibria, Poincare-Hopf, and late applications all use this family. The course ends here because it shows topology acting on behavior, not only on static pictures. A rule, a mechanism, or an arrow field becomes something the earlier shape tools can inspect.
depth.failure_mode: The common failure is to model the state space carelessly. If the states, boundaries, forbidden positions, or allowed motions are wrong, the topological conclusion may no longer describe the physical system being studied at all. The page must therefore treat modeling as part of the proof, not as a preface before the real argument.

essay: Motion-through-state arguments are the course's bridge from shapes to behavior. Instead of following a mechanism directly, the method lists its possible states and treats each state as a point in a new space. A motion is then a path through that space. A rule becomes a map of the space to itself. A forbidden physical arrangement becomes a wall, hole, or missing region in the state space.

This family explains why fixed points, vector fields, configuration spaces, and physical examples belong with surface topology. They are all ways of asking what behavior the shape of possibility permits. The course does not need every equation of motion to say something meaningful. If the state space has the right obstruction, some positions, coincidences, defects, or blocked motions are forced before detailed solving begins.

From first principles, the method replaces time with possibility. Instead of asking where the system goes at every instant, ask what one complete state is, what states are allowed, and what paths through the state space would represent legal motion. A fixed point becomes self-agreement of a rule on that space. An equilibrium becomes a zero of an arrow field. A blocked motion becomes a missing path. A forbidden collision becomes a removed point, wall, or region that can split the space of possible motions.

The same tools now speak about behavior because behavior has been turned into a shape of possibilities. Deformation tracks legal motion through possible states. Invariants record what cannot change along such motion. Fixed-point theorems and index sums force special states. The late applications are not separate from the earlier paper-strip lessons; they use the same object, move, protected fact, and consequence pattern.

The detail that keeps the method honest is modeling. The state space must contain the right freedoms and remove the right forbidden states. One point must not hide two physically different situations unless the problem truly treats them as the same. A path must mean a legal continuous motion, not merely a line drawn in a convenient diagram. If that translation is wrong, the topological conclusion may be true about the model but false about the physical situation. Modeling is therefore part of the proof, not a story attached before the proof begins.

contract.input: A physical or dynamical situation whose direct motion is too complicated to follow point by point. The input must be translated into complete states, not a loose physical impression or a picture that forgets a real degree of freedom. One point of the state space must mean one complete possible situation.
contract.action: Build the space of possible states, remove forbidden states, translate motion into paths or rules, and apply fixed-point, index, or obstruction reasoning there. The action moves from behavior to the shape of possibility while preserving the original freedoms, contacts, boundaries, and forbidden positions.
contract.evidence: The protected evidence is the shape of possibility: a barrier, hole, forced self-agreement, index total, or missing legal path. That evidence constrains behavior without solving every trajectory because each point still means a real possible state and each path still means a legal gradual motion.
contract.output: The output is a constraint on the original motion, such as an unavoidable state, blocked motion, equilibrium, required defect, or forced self-agreement. The conclusion must translate back to the physical setup in the same terms used to build the state space.

math_why.big_picture: The mathematical heart of the course is the search for facts that survive honest change. Exact length, exact angle, and exact placement often change too easily for the question being asked. Tokieda's course asks for a better handle: a gluing rule, boundary order, hole, signed meeting, fixed point, state-space path, or total index. Those handles let a person prove something when direct measurement or direct solving is the wrong tool. This matters because many real problems are too large, too moving, or too constrained to solve by drawing every detail. Topology asks which detail still matters after the harmless details have moved away.
math_why.first_principles: Start with an object or motion that is too complicated to inspect directly. Name the object before naming the technique: a strip is a strip with an end-gluing rule, a map is a rule from one space back into that same space, and a mechanism is a space of allowed states. Then decide which changes leave the real question unchanged. Move the object only under that contract, track the feature that did not change, and let the simplified picture answer the original question. The first-principles habit is ordinary: say what thing is being studied, what freedom it has, what it is forbidden to do, and what fact remains after the allowed change.
math_why.important_detail: The allowed changes are the whole contract. A result is only as strong as the promise that the change did not cut, glue, pass through a forbidden object, erase a boundary, reverse a side rule, omit a state variable, or invent a sign convention. The course spends so much time on ordinary position, orientation, boundaries, and signs because those details keep a short explanation from silently changing the problem. A plain explanation must therefore slow down at the permission step. If the permission is wrong, the final sentence may be clear, confident, and false.
math_why.principle: Topology and geometry become decisive when local details are organized so that the whole shape has fewer choices than it appears to have. Local patches may look free. Local arrows may look adjustable. Local crossings may look removable. But the completed object can force a side reversal, a nonzero count, a fixed point, or a defect. A named object plus a named rule of change can turn many small freedoms into one unavoidable conclusion. That is why the course keeps moving between pictures and counts: the picture shows what can be tried, while the count or obstruction shows what cannot be escaped.
math_why.concepts_matter: Each core concept protects a different kind of evidence. Deformation protects the question while the picture moves. Invariants remember exactly what survived the permitted moves. Euler characteristic turns a surface into stable bookkeeping. Intersection number records meetings only after signs share an orientation rule. Fixed points turn rules into forced self-agreement inside one space. Configuration space turns motion into paths through allowed states. Vector-field index turns local arrow failures into a count that the whole surface controls. Together these ideas explain why topology matters beyond naming shapes: it gives a way to reason about routes, barriers, possible states, stable counts, and forced behavior.
math_why.reader_path: This course is not a vocabulary list. The path is: first see a physical surprise, then name the object, then name the legal motion, then ask what fact survives that motion, then build a count or obstruction, then state exactly what kind of conclusion follows. The companion links lectures, concepts, themes, subthemes, and method families in both directions so that every term points back to the work it performs. Read each page by asking why the idea was needed at all. If the page cannot say what problem became easier, what false shortcut was blocked, or what application became possible, it is not yet explaining the course deeply enough.

lecture_spine.object: A strip made by gluing its ends after a half-turn.
lecture_spine.plain_question: Can a surface look ordinary in every small patch while carrying a whole-surface rule that changes what side means?
lecture_spine.legal_move: Follow, mark, or cut the strip without pretending the glued edge rule has disappeared.
lecture_spine.surviving_fact: A full trip around the strip reverses the local side choice instead of returning it unchanged.
lecture_spine.why_later: This is the first warning against local-only thinking. Later orientation, manifolds, vector fields, and surface classification all use the same gap between small-patch behavior and whole-object behavior.

lecture_spine.object: Curves inside a disk with boundary points held in their circular order.
lecture_spine.plain_question: When can a messy drawing be replaced by a cleaner one without changing the problem it was meant to answer?
lecture_spine.legal_move: Slide and bend curves while keeping endpoints fixed in order and while preventing forbidden crossings.
lecture_spine.surviving_fact: Boundary order and the no-crossing rule survive the redraw, so an unavoidable crossing belongs to the original setup.
lecture_spine.why_later: This lecture makes deformation into a proof method. Intersection number, fixed points, and vector-field cleanup all rely on this same contract: move the picture, but protect the question.

lecture_spine.object: Spaces built from choices, identifications, local patches, and controlled replacements.
lecture_spine.plain_question: How can a complicated space be made from simple instructions instead of being drawn all at once?
lecture_spine.legal_move: Build by product, quotient, manifold charts, or surgery while keeping the construction rule visible.
lecture_spine.surviving_fact: The rule of construction decides the routes, holes, sides, and local neighborhoods available in the finished space.
lecture_spine.why_later: Later theorems are only as honest as the spaces they act on. This lecture gives the raw building tools for configuration spaces, graphs of maps, quotient surfaces, and surface surgery.

lecture_spine.object: A square whose marked edges are read as travel instructions for a finished surface.
lecture_spine.plain_question: How can the same flat drawing represent different worlds depending on which edge exits are declared identical?
lecture_spine.legal_move: Read each edge identification as part of the object, including whether direction is preserved or reversed.
lecture_spine.surviving_fact: The gluing rule determines whether paths close, whether sides remain consistent, and whether the drawn boundary is a true boundary.
lecture_spine.why_later: This is the plain entrance to quotient thinking. It prepares the reader for manifolds and for later situations where a rule, not visual appearance, defines the mathematical object.

lecture_spine.object: Surfaces broken into standard features such as handles, crosscaps, and boundary components.
lecture_spine.plain_question: What does it mean to say two surfaces are the same when their drawings can look very different?
lecture_spine.legal_move: Cut, glue, and simplify under controlled surface operations while tracking the features those operations preserve.
lecture_spine.surviving_fact: Orientability, boundary behavior, and durable surface pieces remain as the evidence used to classify the surface.
lecture_spine.why_later: This gives Euler characteristic and orientation a home. Later local counts only have force because they live on a surface whose global type has been understood.

lecture_spine.object: Subspaces placed inside a surrounding space with only so much room to avoid one another.
lecture_spine.plain_question: When is a meeting between objects an accident of the drawing, and when is it forced by dimension and position?
lecture_spine.legal_move: Move objects into ordinary position so meetings are clean and separate, without changing the surrounding problem.
lecture_spine.surviving_fact: After accidental coincidences are removed, the remaining pattern of meetings can carry real information.
lecture_spine.why_later: This lecture supplies the discipline needed before signs can be assigned. Intersection number only works after meetings are clean enough to count honestly.

lecture_spine.object: A physical balance condition that changes continuously as the setup moves.
lecture_spine.plain_question: How can a special state be forced even when we cannot calculate its exact location?
lecture_spine.legal_move: Track the changing condition continuously and ask whether it can pass from one side of a requirement to another without meeting it.
lecture_spine.surviving_fact: Continuity prevents the condition from jumping over the balance state.
lecture_spine.why_later: This is the physical doorway into existence proofs. It prepares fixed points, intersections with the diagonal, and equilibria as forced special states rather than computed answers.

lecture_spine.object: Clean intersections between oriented objects, equipped with plus and minus signs.
lecture_spine.plain_question: How can a count survive when crossings can appear or disappear during legal motion?
lecture_spine.legal_move: Assign signs using a consistent orientation rule and allow only deformations where pair creation is inspected.
lecture_spine.surviving_fact: Opposite-signed pairs can be born or die without changing the signed total.
lecture_spine.why_later: This is the counting engine for the second half of the course. Fixed points and vector-field index both reuse the idea that local events become evidence when cancellation is controlled.

lecture_spine.object: The graph of a map compared with the diagonal of self-agreement.
lecture_spine.plain_question: How can the equation that says 'the output equals the input' become a visible geometric meeting?
lecture_spine.legal_move: Translate the rule into its graph in input-output space and compare it with the diagonal without changing what equality means.
lecture_spine.surviving_fact: A meeting of graph and diagonal is exactly a fixed point of the original map.
lecture_spine.why_later: This converts rules into shapes. Brouwer and later dynamics become easier to read because existence can now be treated as forced intersection rather than hidden algebra.

lecture_spine.object: A continuous self-map of a closed ball, including its filled interior and boundary.
lecture_spine.plain_question: Why can a filled shape force at least one point to stay put under every continuous rule of the right kind?
lecture_spine.legal_move: Keep the domain filled, keep the boundary condition honest, and forbid jumps in the rule.
lecture_spine.surviving_fact: The ball gives no continuous escape plan that moves every point away from itself at once.
lecture_spine.why_later: This is the strongest plain example of shape forcing existence. It also teaches the necessary caution: the theorem depends on the exact space and the exact kind of rule.

lecture_spine.object: A vector field, meaning an arrow assigned to each point of a surface or state space.
lecture_spine.plain_question: What can be learned about motion without solving every path of motion?
lecture_spine.legal_move: Study the arrow pattern and isolate the points where the arrow vanishes.
lecture_spine.surviving_fact: An equilibrium carries more information than its location; nearby arrows turn around it in a countable way.
lecture_spine.why_later: This shifts the course from fixed places to motion laws. It prepares index as the local evidence attached to a failure of motion.

lecture_spine.object: Indices assigned to isolated vector-field defects by reading nearby arrow turning.
lecture_spine.plain_question: How can many local motion failures add up to one whole-surface demand?
lecture_spine.legal_move: Clean the field to isolated defects, read the turning around each one, and add the signed local counts.
lecture_spine.surviving_fact: Defects may move or split, but the total signed index is constrained by the surface.
lecture_spine.why_later: This is the immediate bridge from local dynamics to Poincare-Hopf. It shows why the whole surface, not one defect, controls the conclusion.

lecture_spine.object: A vector field on a surface, with all isolated defects counted together.
lecture_spine.plain_question: Why must the total defect of a motion pattern answer to the shape that carries it?
lecture_spine.legal_move: Use Poincare-Hopf only after the field is clean enough and the surface carrying it is the right one.
lecture_spine.surviving_fact: The sum of local indices equals the Euler characteristic of the surface.
lecture_spine.why_later: This gathers the course's main chain: surface bookkeeping, signs, local defects, and global constraint. The hairy-ball idea is one visible consequence, not the whole story.

lecture_spine.object: A physical or moving system translated into a space of possible states.
lecture_spine.plain_question: How can topology say something useful about an application before every motion equation is solved?
lecture_spine.legal_move: Choose the state space honestly, include the real freedoms, exclude the real forbidden states, and then apply the theorem to that model.
lecture_spine.surviving_fact: Barriers, holes, fixed points, and index totals in the state space become constraints on the original system.
lecture_spine.why_later: This tests the whole course outside its cleanest surface examples. It shows that first-principles modeling is part of the mathematics, not a preliminary story.

lecture_spine.object: The whole course as a chain of picture-based reasoning moves.
lecture_spine.plain_question: What single habit connects strips, surfaces, intersections, fixed points, and vector fields?
lecture_spine.legal_move: Translate each situation into objects, allowed moves, protected evidence, and a conclusion that follows from that evidence.
lecture_spine.surviving_fact: The same reasoning pattern survives across settings: build the right picture, move it legally, count what survives, and let the shape force the answer.
lecture_spine.why_later: This is the final reader standard for the companion. A page is deep enough only when the reader can say what object was made, what move was legal, what fact survived, and why that fact forces the conclusion.

source_nuance_repairs.do_not_claim: Do not let product, quotient, manifold, or surgery appear as unexplained vocabulary that merely decorates the paragraph. The independent choices, imposed identifications, local test, or replacement boundary must be visible before the formal word is allowed to shorten the sentence.
source_nuance_repairs.reviewer_question: Evidence check: reconstruct the space from the rule alone by naming the choices, identifications, local patches, or replacement boundary before using product, quotient, manifold, or surgery as a shortcut for the completed construction.

source_nuance_repairs.caption_hazard: Gluing and boundary words can make the drawn square look like the object itself. Captions may not signal that arrows and labels are instructions for building a surface, so the reader may reason from the wrong object.
source_nuance_repairs.safe_claim: The supported claim is that edge identifications are instructions for the finished surface. They decide where a traveler re-enters, whether an apparent border remains a border, and whether a local direction choice survives a full loop.
source_nuance_repairs.repair_move: When a page reasons from a square, add a sentence that applies the gluing rule before drawing conclusions. The repair should say what points become identical and how paths, boundary, orientation, or apparent edges behave after the identification.
source_nuance_repairs.do_not_claim: Do not call the unglued drawing the final surface or treat its outside edges as physical borders by default. It is a code for a surface that exists only after the stated identifications are actually made.
source_nuance_repairs.reviewer_question: Evidence check: say which points become identical, how a path crosses the glued edge afterward, and which boundary or orientation claim would be false if the flat square were read literally instead of as instructions.

source_nuance_repairs.caption_hazard: Classification, orientable, handle, and boundary can sound like a naming exercise. The course point is not to memorize surface labels, but to see which features remain after cutting, gluing, stretching, and redrawing have removed accidental appearances.
source_nuance_repairs.safe_claim: The supported claim is that surface classification is about durable evidence after legal rearrangement. Handles preserve route choices, boundary pieces preserve edge behavior, and orientability records whether side choices can agree globally across the whole surface.
source_nuance_repairs.repair_move: If a paragraph lists surface types, add the test that tells them apart. Ask what happens to loops, sides, handles, or boundary under legal changes, and explain why those checks survive a different drawing of the same surface.
source_nuance_repairs.do_not_claim: Do not imply every visual difference creates a new surface type or that a surface name by itself explains the case. Classification earns its force because many drawings represent the same underlying surface once the surviving features have been checked.
source_nuance_repairs.reviewer_question: Evidence check: name the surviving feature after the cuts and gluings, explain how a different drawing would still carry it, and do not treat a surface name as the proof that the classification has been earned.

source_nuance_repairs.caption_hazard: Dimension and submanifold language can sound abstract before the physical question is clear. The lecture asks an everyday room question first: when two moving things have enough freedom, can a small legal nudge separate accidental meetings from unavoidable ones?
source_nuance_repairs.safe_claim: The supported claim is that the lecture uses dimension and ordinary position to separate accidental contact from evidence. After a legal nudge, some meetings disappear, while clean remaining meetings can be counted, signed, or inspected without depending on a messy drawing.
source_nuance_repairs.repair_move: When a sentence mentions generic position, add the ordinary picture it creates. The repair should describe clean meetings, separated events, and counts or signs that can be assigned after the legal nudge without changing the original placement question.
source_nuance_repairs.do_not_claim: Do not treat every visible meeting as forced or every disappearance as meaningless. The page must distinguish a removable accident from a meeting protected by the setup after the objects have been placed in ordinary position.
source_nuance_repairs.reviewer_question: Evidence check: identify the accident removed by the small nudge, the meeting pattern that remains, and the reason the nudge preserves the original placement question instead of quietly replacing it with a different problem.

source_nuance_repairs.caption_hazard: Center-of-gravity language can pull the reader toward physics alone. The mathematical point is the forced passage through a special state under continuous change, where a watched quantity cannot jump across the required balance condition.
source_nuance_repairs.safe_claim: The supported claim is that the balance demonstration gives a first existence argument. A continuously changing quantity cannot pass from one side of the required condition to the other without meeting it somewhere, even if the lecture does not compute where.
source_nuance_repairs.repair_move: If a paragraph stays with balance intuition, add the quantity being watched, the two sides of the comparison, and the special equality that no-jump motion forces. Then state that the argument proves existence, not a recipe for finding the place.
source_nuance_repairs.do_not_claim: Do not say the physical demonstration proves every later theorem or replaces their assumptions. It supplies the shared pattern of continuous motion, comparison, and forced meeting; each later theorem still needs its own object, domain, and rule.
source_nuance_repairs.reviewer_question: Evidence check: identify the changing quantity, the condition it cannot skip, and the exact claim limit. The repaired claim proves the existence of a special state rather than claiming a computation of its location.

source_nuance_repairs.caption_hazard: Positive and negative intersection words can be copied as signs without explaining where signs come from. The source risk is arithmetic without orientation, where plus and minus look like decoration instead of evidence tied to local direction.
source_nuance_repairs.safe_claim: The supported claim is that the lecture repairs raw crossing counts by giving clean meetings signs. Pair events created or removed during legal motion then contribute no net change, so the signed total becomes the quantity worth protecting.
source_nuance_repairs.repair_move: When a page uses plus and minus intersections, add the shared orientation or local direction rule. Then show one birth or death event where the two signs cancel, so the arithmetic is tied to a visible motion.
source_nuance_repairs.do_not_claim: Do not call the raw number of crossings invariant or let sign language stand alone. The protected candidate is the signed total after the page has explained clean meetings, orientation, and why pair cancellation is allowed.
source_nuance_repairs.reviewer_question: Evidence check: show where the signs come from, why a newly born pair contributes opposite signs, and what legal motion leaves the signed total unchanged while allowing the raw number of crossings to change.

source_nuance_repairs.caption_hazard: This lecture has a missing-caption middle part, so any claim about the full transition from maps to fixed points needs extra caution. The available source supports the surrounding arc, not every hidden sentence or intermediate explanation.
source_nuance_repairs.safe_claim: The supported claim is the graph-diagonal translation. A rule becomes its graph, the diagonal records self-agreement, and a meeting between them is a fixed point, while the missing-caption gap limits stronger claims about the lecture's exact route.
source_nuance_repairs.repair_move: If a sentence depends on the absent middle caption, weaken it to the recovered structure. Stay with map, graph, diagonal, self-agreement, and controlled intersection language, and mark any bridge beyond that as course-arc inference.
source_nuance_repairs.do_not_claim: Do not present the missing section as transcript-verified or quote it as if the words were available. Mark it as course-arc inference unless a human check of the video supplies stronger evidence for the exact transition.
source_nuance_repairs.reviewer_question: Evidence check: justify the claim from recovered captions and visible lecture structure, and keep it at graph, diagonal, and self-agreement unless a human check supplies the missing middle evidence needed for a stronger statement.

source_nuance_repairs.caption_hazard: Brouwer, closed ball, boundary, and continuous can make the theorem sound like a slogan. The reader needs the filled space, the rule that sends it back into itself, and the no-jump condition before the name carries meaning.
source_nuance_repairs.safe_claim: The supported claim is Brouwer's fixed-point contract in plain terms. A continuous rule from a closed filled ball back into itself cannot move every point away from itself; at least one point must be sent to itself.
source_nuance_repairs.repair_move: When Brouwer is named, add the four checks: closed filled ball, map back into itself, continuity, and fixed-point conclusion. Also say what the theorem does not supply: a location, uniqueness, or solved motion path.
source_nuance_repairs.do_not_claim: Do not use Brouwer as a general statement that every motion has a fixed point or that every process returns somewhere. The object, self-map rule, closedness, and continuity condition are part of the theorem's force.
source_nuance_repairs.reviewer_question: Evidence check: name the closed filled space, the self-map rule, the no-jump condition, and the conclusion limit. The claim is at least one fixed point, not its location, uniqueness, or an algorithm for finding it.

source_nuance_repairs.caption_hazard: Vector field, equilibrium, differential equation, and index can collapse into one motion vocabulary. The lecture separates the arrows, the vanishing points, and what can be learned from nearby turning before any path is solved.
source_nuance_repairs.safe_claim: The supported claim is that vector fields let the course study motion by reading an arrow pattern. Where arrows vanish, how nearby arrows turn, and what the local pattern forces can be studied before trajectories are solved.
source_nuance_repairs.repair_move: If a paragraph says the system has an equilibrium, add how the arrow field behaves nearby and what question remains after the point is found. The repair should distinguish locating a zero from understanding the local turn pattern.
source_nuance_repairs.do_not_claim: Do not treat an equilibrium as the same object as a fixed point of a map unless the map or motion law has been named. A vanishing arrow, a return point, and a solved trajectory are related but not interchangeable.
source_nuance_repairs.reviewer_question: Evidence check: point to the field, isolate the vanishing point, walk around it in nearby arrows, and keep that local evidence separate from a fixed point of an unnamed map or a solution path not yet computed.

source_nuance_repairs.caption_hazard: Index and Euler characteristic can sound like two names for one number. The lecture is about two levels of evidence: local arrow turning near each defect and the whole-surface account those local entries must eventually match.
source_nuance_repairs.safe_claim: The supported claim is that isolated vector-field defects carry local signed evidence. Only the total over all defects on the same surface, under the needed boundary or cleanup assumptions, is ready to be compared with the surface account.
source_nuance_repairs.repair_move: When a page adds indices, add the scope of the sum. Every isolated defect on the same surface must be included, and the boundary condition, cleanup step, or reason no defect is missing must be named.
source_nuance_repairs.do_not_claim: Do not compare one local index directly with Euler characteristic as if it were the whole theorem. The comparison belongs to the completed same-surface ledger after all local defects have been counted under the right assumptions.
source_nuance_repairs.reviewer_question: Evidence check: distinguish one defect's local turning from the complete same-surface index sum, then name the surface number that total is allowed to meet and the condition that makes the comparison legal.

source_nuance_repairs.caption_hazard: Poincare-Hopf and hairy-ball language can become a memorable phrase without the bookkeeping contract. The theorem needs a chosen surface, a vector field on it, isolated defects, local index assignments, and a complete total.
source_nuance_repairs.safe_claim: The supported claim is the Poincare-Hopf ledger. After all isolated defects of a vector field on the same surface are counted with local index, their total is tied to that surface's Euler characteristic.
source_nuance_repairs.repair_move: If a sentence says topology predicts motion, add the mechanism. List the defects, assign local indices, add them over the same surface, and compare that complete total with the surface invariant rather than speaking in broad prediction language.
source_nuance_repairs.do_not_claim: Do not say the theorem solves the differential equation or gives exact motion paths. It constrains possible defects and equilibria before exact solutions are known, and only after the theorem's surface and defect conditions are in place.
source_nuance_repairs.reviewer_question: Evidence check: name the surface, list the complete defect account, state how local indices are assigned, and say what stronger motion claim the theorem does not provide beyond the total constraint.

source_nuance_repairs.caption_hazard: Applications, rotation, state space, and dynamical-system language can make examples look unrelated. The source risk is missing the shared idea: replace the physical story with a space of possible states, then study the shape and forbidden regions of that space.
source_nuance_repairs.safe_claim: The supported claim is that applications reuse the earlier method only after translation. Build the state space, remove forbidden states, interpret paths as legal motions, and read the topological constraint inside that model.
source_nuance_repairs.repair_move: When an application appears, add the model behind it. Say what one point of the state space represents, what movement inside that space means, which states are forbidden, and which earlier course constraint is being reused.
source_nuance_repairs.do_not_claim: Do not treat a physical example as automatically solved by topology or skip the modeling step. The topological claim only applies after the model matches the allowed states, forbidden states, freedoms, and boundary conditions.
source_nuance_repairs.reviewer_question: Evidence check: say what one state records, which physical impossibilities were removed, how a path in the model becomes a real motion, and which claim would overreach the model because the translation was not justified.

source_nuance_repairs.caption_hazard: The final pictorial-thinking summary can sound like an aesthetic preference. The course is not saying pictures are nice; it is saying pictures can carry rules, allowed moves, forbidden moves, protected evidence, and claim limits.
source_nuance_repairs.safe_claim: The supported claim is that the final lecture gathers a reusable proof habit. Make the object visible, state the allowed and forbidden moves, protect the evidence, then draw only the conclusion that the evidence can carry.
source_nuance_repairs.repair_move: If a conclusion says pictorial thinking matters, add the proof contract a picture must satisfy. Name the object, allowed move, forbidden move, protected fact, failure test, and the exact claim boundary before praising the picture.
source_nuance_repairs.do_not_claim: Do not reduce the course to visual intuition or say the pictures replace proof. The pictures expose constraints that can be audited: route order, gluing rules, signed counts, fixed-point meetings, defect totals, and model limits.
source_nuance_repairs.reviewer_question: Evidence check: use the final summary on an earlier lecture by naming its object, legal move, protected fact, failure condition, and claim boundary, then state what the picture alone would not prove.

concept_dependencies.stage: From local patch evidence to whole-surface behavior
concept_dependencies.plain: A small patch can look ordinary while the whole surface changes what routes and sides mean.
concept_dependencies.why: This is the first dependency in the course. Before a reader can trust later surface arguments, they need to see that local evidence is not enough. Quotient rules and manifold language give that local-versus-global gap a precise form.
concept_dependencies.reader_check: Can I say what is locally ordinary, and what whole-surface fact is still undecided?

concept_dependencies.stage: From legal motion to protected mathematical evidence in proof
concept_dependencies.plain: A picture may move, but the proof needs a fact that moves with it unchanged.
concept_dependencies.why: Deformation by itself is only motion. Generic position cleans the picture enough to inspect it. Invariant and parity add evidence: something survives the motion and can rule out a desired ending.
concept_dependencies.reader_check: What exact move is legal, and what fact is still true after that move?

concept_dependencies.stage: From built spaces to durable surface classification rules
concept_dependencies.plain: A space built from choices, identifications, or replacements can be sorted by durable surface features.
concept_dependencies.why: Products make choice-spaces, quotients make sameness rules, and surgery changes a surface under boundary control. Those operations prepare the reader to count faces, track orientation, and name the surface by what survives simplification.
concept_dependencies.reader_check: What construction rule made this space, and which surface features did that rule create or preserve?

concept_dependencies.stage: From surface ledger to stable whole-shape number
concept_dependencies.plain: A surface count first looks like bookkeeping, then becomes a number that can control geometry and motion.
concept_dependencies.why: Triangulation makes a soft surface finite enough to count. Euler characteristic shows that the final account does not belong to one mesh. Later, Gauss-Bonnet and Poincare-Hopf use that same whole-surface number to constrain turning and vector-field defects.
concept_dependencies.reader_check: Is this number attached to one drawing, or to the surface after redrawings and refinements?

concept_dependencies.stage: From clean meetings to signed obstruction under deformation
concept_dependencies.plain: Clean meetings can be assigned signs, and the signed total can force a later meeting to exist.
concept_dependencies.why: Generic position separates meetings. Orientation gives signs meaning. Winding and linking train the idea of a stable relation. Intersection number combines these into a count that survives legal motion, then fixed-point theory uses meetings between graph and diagonal.
concept_dependencies.reader_check: Are the meetings clean, and do the signs come from a real direction rule?

concept_dependencies.stage: From a rule to forced self-agreement inside space
concept_dependencies.plain: A rule becomes a shape in a larger space; self-agreement becomes a meeting with the diagonal.
concept_dependencies.why: Product space holds input and output together. Duality allows the rule to be redrawn as a graph. Intersection number explains why a graph may be unable to avoid the diagonal. Brouwer is the closed-ball version where the space itself blocks total escape.
concept_dependencies.reader_check: What is the graph, what is the diagonal, and why would their meeting mean a fixed point?

concept_dependencies.stage: From arrow-field failure to signed index around defects
concept_dependencies.plain: A place where motion stops can be read by how nearby arrows turn around it.
concept_dependencies.why: Fixed points teach forced special states. Equilibrium turns that idea into a failure of an arrow field. Generic position keeps failures isolated. Vector-field index makes each failure countable, and Poincare-Hopf adds those counts over the whole surface.
concept_dependencies.reader_check: Is the defect isolated, and what do the arrows do on a small loop around it?

concept_dependencies.stage: From state-space model to physical application constraints
concept_dependencies.plain: A physical problem becomes usable only after its possible states are turned into the right mathematical space.
concept_dependencies.why: Configuration space lists the possible states. Fixed points and Poincare-Hopf supply forced-behavior tools. Duality and invariants keep the translation honest by asking whether the new picture still means the original physical question.
concept_dependencies.reader_check: Does the state space include the real freedoms and exclude the real forbidden states?

transfer_lab_cases.title: Rubber band around a mug handle
transfer_lab_cases.situation: A rubber band is looped around the handle of a mug. You can stretch the band and slide it on the mug, but you cannot cut it or pass it through the ceramic.
transfer_lab_cases.object: The object is the loop together with the mug handle acting as an obstacle. The exact roundness of the band is not the issue. What matters is the relationship between the closed loop and the hole through the handle.
transfer_lab_cases.allowed_move: The allowed move is a continuous sliding and stretching of the loop while the band stays uncut and never crosses through the handle. The band may get longer, thinner, or uglier; it may not pass through ceramic or open itself.
transfer_lab_cases.protected_fact: The protected fact is whether the loop is linked around the handle. That relation survives many changes of shape because the only moves that would remove it are exactly the moves the problem forbids.
transfer_lab_cases.course_bridge: This transfers the knot-and-link habit from the course: do not trust the drawing's neatness; ask what relationship cannot be removed by legal deformation. The mug handle plays the role of forbidden matter, and the band plays the role of a loop whose route memory matters.
transfer_lab_cases.wrong_transfer: A shallow response says the band looks circular or messy. That talks about geometry of the drawing, not the topological relation that blocks removal. It also misses the illegal move: pulling the band through the handle or cutting it open.
transfer_lab_cases.reader_task: Explain whether the band can be freed without cutting it, name the exact move that would be illegal, and say which relationship survives every legal stretch.

transfer_lab_cases.title: Two walking routes around a fountain
transfer_lab_cases.situation: Two routes across a plaza start and end at the same gates, but one route goes around a fenced fountain and the other does not.
transfer_lab_cases.object: The object is not the pavement drawing alone. It is the plaza with the fenced region removed and the two paths inside the remaining space. The fence changes the space because it creates a place the path is not allowed to cross.
transfer_lab_cases.allowed_move: The allowed move is to slide a route through open walking space while keeping its endpoints at the gates and never crossing the fence. The path may wiggle, shorten, or lengthen, but the endpoints and forbidden region define the same route problem.
transfer_lab_cases.protected_fact: The protected fact is whether the route winds around the missing region. A fenced hole can block one path from being changed into the other because any attempted slide would have to cross the fence or move an endpoint.
transfer_lab_cases.course_bridge: This is the same first-principles move as loops on surfaces: the missing region changes which deformations are legal. The course habit is to read the obstacle as part of the object, not as decoration in the drawing.
transfer_lab_cases.wrong_transfer: A shallow response says both paths are just lines between the same gates. That ignores the obstacle that makes the state space different and treats endpoint agreement as enough by itself.
transfer_lab_cases.reader_task: Decide whether one route can be deformed into the other while respecting the fence, say what the fence contributes to the proof, and name the illegal shortcut that would make the routes look equivalent.

transfer_lab_cases.title: Matching arrows on a weather map
transfer_lab_cases.situation: A small weather map shows wind arrows around a calm point. Nearby arrows turn as you walk around the calm point.
transfer_lab_cases.object: The object is the arrow field near an isolated calm point, together with a small loop around that point. The calm point is not just a dot; it is a place where the arrow field fails, and the surrounding arrows are the evidence.
transfer_lab_cases.allowed_move: The allowed move is to clean or redraw nearby arrows without removing the calm point from the loop or dragging another calm point inside. The loop must continue to isolate the same failure so the turning account is about one defect.
transfer_lab_cases.protected_fact: The protected fact is the total turning of the arrows during one walk around the loop. That turning can survive redrawings even when individual arrows are sketched differently.
transfer_lab_cases.course_bridge: This transfers vector-field index from the course: local arrow behavior can become signed evidence without solving the motion everywhere. The everyday map becomes mathematical only after the reader walks around the defect and reads the surrounding arrows.
transfer_lab_cases.wrong_transfer: A shallow response tries to predict the full weather. The course idea only needs the local turning account around the defect. It also must not count every calm-looking point unless the point is isolated and has a readable surrounding pattern.
transfer_lab_cases.reader_task: Walk around the calm point in words, say what has to stay isolated before an index-like count is meaningful, and state what this local count does not predict.

transfer_lab_cases.title: Moving a sofa through a hallway
transfer_lab_cases.situation: A sofa must move from one room to another through a hallway without hitting the walls. The sofa can rotate and slide, but cannot pass through walls.
transfer_lab_cases.object: The object is the space of all allowed sofa positions and rotations, not just one drawing of the hallway. One point in that space must record enough information to know where the sofa is and how it is turned.
transfer_lab_cases.allowed_move: The allowed move is a continuous path through allowed states where every intermediate position avoids collision. The sofa cannot jump through a tight corner, and the model cannot forget rotation if rotation is part of the physical motion.
transfer_lab_cases.protected_fact: The protected fact is whether the start state and end state lie in the same connected region of allowed states. If a wall or narrow turn separates those regions, no continuous legal motion connects the two poses.
transfer_lab_cases.course_bridge: This transfers configuration-space modeling: a motion problem becomes a route problem in the space of possible states. The course idea is not to stare harder at the hallway, but to build the right state space and inspect its allowed paths.
transfer_lab_cases.wrong_transfer: A shallow response stares only at the floor plan. The proof needs the larger space that records both location and angle. It also has to remove collision states before claiming a route exists.
transfer_lab_cases.reader_task: Name what one point of the state space represents, what would count as a forbidden state, and how a path in that space translates back into real sofa motion.

transfer_lab_cases.title: Stirring coffee in a cup
transfer_lab_cases.situation: A spoon stirs coffee inside a round cup, and after the motion every bit of coffee has moved somewhere in the same cup.
transfer_lab_cases.object: The object is the filled cup as a disk-like region and the rule sending each starting point to its ending point. The rule, not the stirring story by itself, is what fixed-point thinking inspects.
transfer_lab_cases.allowed_move: The allowed move is a continuous self-map of the filled region, with no point sent outside the cup. Nearby starting points must end nearby, and the final positions must still live inside the same filled region.
transfer_lab_cases.protected_fact: The protected fact is that a continuous self-map of the right kind of filled region cannot avoid some self-agreement. The conclusion is about at least one starting point matching its ending point, not about all points returning.
transfer_lab_cases.course_bridge: This transfers fixed-point thinking: the question is not where the point is, but why some point must return to itself. The everyday motion becomes course mathematics only after the domain, rule, and self-map condition are named.
transfer_lab_cases.wrong_transfer: A shallow response says every point returns or that the theorem computes the point. The safe conclusion is existence of at least one fixed point, and only after the self-map contract has been checked.
transfer_lab_cases.reader_task: State the domain, the rule, and the exact conclusion without pretending to locate the fixed point or claiming that every bit of coffee returns.

transfer_lab_cases.title: Drawing a map on a folded sheet
transfer_lab_cases.situation: A map is drawn on a sheet whose opposite edges are taped together according to arrows. After taping, some apparent edges are no longer edges.
transfer_lab_cases.object: The object is the finished surface created by the taping rule, not the flat sheet before the rule is applied. The arrows and tape are instructions for sameness, so the completed object may have fewer boundaries than the drawing suggests.
transfer_lab_cases.allowed_move: The allowed move is to reason after the edge identifications have been made, treating glued points as the same point. Redrawing the sheet is harmless only if the same identification rule is still being used.
transfer_lab_cases.protected_fact: The protected fact is the route and boundary behavior of the completed surface after the taped edges are treated as one. A path that looks like it hits an edge on paper may continue through the glued edge in the finished surface.
transfer_lab_cases.course_bridge: This transfers quotient-space reading: the drawing is a code, and the gluing rule tells the reader what space the code describes. The course habit is to read the rule before trusting the picture.
transfer_lab_cases.wrong_transfer: A shallow response counts the border of the flat sheet as a real boundary after the taping rule has already removed it. That reasons about the code instead of the finished object.
transfer_lab_cases.reader_task: Say which points become the same point, what boundary claim changes after the identification, and which feature of the flat drawing should no longer be read literally.

transfer_lab_cases.title: Counting dents on a squeezed ball
transfer_lab_cases.situation: A soft ball is squeezed, dented, and redrawn with different patches, but it is never punctured or glued to another piece.
transfer_lab_cases.object: The object is the surface of the ball under legal deformation, not the number of visible dents in one picture. The surface remains the carrier even when its drawing, patching, or local wrinkles change.
transfer_lab_cases.allowed_move: The allowed move is to bend and redraw the surface without tearing, puncturing, or changing how the surface is connected. Changing the cell account is allowed only when it still describes the same surface.
transfer_lab_cases.protected_fact: The protected fact is a whole-surface count such as Euler characteristic, not the raw count of dents or patch lines. Dents may appear or disappear; the useful count is the one designed to survive legal changes to the surface account.
transfer_lab_cases.course_bridge: This transfers the stable-count habit: choose the count designed to survive the legal changes, not the count easiest to see. The everyday squeezed ball becomes a test for separating drawing noise from whole-surface evidence.
transfer_lab_cases.wrong_transfer: A shallow response counts every wrinkle as mathematical evidence. Wrinkles are drawing noise unless the argument says why they survive. The repair is to ask which count remains the same after the surface is redrawn honestly.
transfer_lab_cases.reader_task: Identify one visible count that is not protected, one whole-surface fact that is protected, and the illegal change that would stop the protected fact from applying.

transfer_lab_cases.title: A robot arm avoiding a blocked zone
transfer_lab_cases.situation: A simple arm has two joints and must move from one pose to another while its tip avoids a blocked zone on the table.
transfer_lab_cases.object: The object is the space of joint choices after forbidden choices have been removed. One point records one complete arm pose, including enough joint data to know where the tip is and whether the pose is allowed.
transfer_lab_cases.allowed_move: The allowed move is a continuous path through allowed joint choices, with no intermediate pose entering the blocked zone. The arm may move gradually through joint space, but the path cannot pass through a forbidden pose just because the drawing on the table looks convenient.
transfer_lab_cases.protected_fact: The protected fact is whether the allowed-pose space has a route from the start pose to the target pose. A blocked zone can create a hole, wall, or disconnected region in the space of choices.
transfer_lab_cases.course_bridge: This transfers late-course application thinking: topology studies the shape of possible states before detailed motion equations are solved. The course does not need every control input before it can ask whether the allowed state space has a route.
transfer_lab_cases.wrong_transfer: A shallow response draws only the arm in physical space. The topological question lives in the space of all allowed joint choices, after forbidden poses have been removed and real freedoms have been kept.
transfer_lab_cases.reader_task: Describe one complete state of the arm, explain what removed states do to the route question, and say what conclusion would overclaim beyond the state-space model.

repair_clinic_cases.title: Mobius strip as a visual surprise
repair_clinic_cases.flawed_explanation: The Mobius strip is surprising because it has one side, so topology is about weird shapes.
repair_clinic_cases.why_it_fails: This sentence remembers the punchline but loses the method. It does not say what object is being tested, what motion or walk reveals the fact, or why local patches fail to show the whole behavior. It also turns the course into a collection of surprising objects instead of a way to ask what survives a full journey around an object.
repair_clinic_cases.repair_move: Replace the surprise with the walk-around account. Say what a mark or traveler does on the strip and what returns changed after one complete trip. Then contrast that full-trip evidence with the local view, where every small patch still looks ordinary.
repair_clinic_cases.strong_version: A Mobius strip exposes a first problem: a local view of the paper does not reveal the whole-side behavior. When a mark is followed around the full strip, the route returns with side information that an ordinary band would not have. The course uses this to show why whole-shape facts can be invisible in small pieces, and why a topological explanation must name the completed object rather than only the part visible at one moment.
repair_clinic_cases.reviewer_test: Evidence test: explain the one-side claim by describing a full trip around the strip, naming what changes after the trip, and saying why a small local patch could not have shown that fact.

repair_clinic_cases.title: Invariant as any number that stays useful
repair_clinic_cases.flawed_explanation: An invariant is a number we calculate from a shape, and it helps us compare examples.
repair_clinic_cases.why_it_fails: The sentence sounds plausible but avoids the main test. A number is not an invariant because it is useful once; it earns the role by surviving the allowed changes in the problem. The weak sentence also hides the difference between a raw visible count and a count that has been designed to ignore harmless changes.
repair_clinic_cases.repair_move: Name the legal move that threatens the count, then explain why the proposed number survives that move or how signs, parity, or cancellation repair the count. The repair should include one local event, such as a pair of crossings being born, so the reader can see the survival test happen.
repair_clinic_cases.strong_version: An invariant is evidence designed to survive the moves the problem allows. If two crossings are born as an opposite pair, a raw crossing count changes, but a signed total can stay fixed. The invariant carries the same information from one legal drawing to another, so a different value can rule out a proposed deformation without trusting either drawing's temporary clutter.
repair_clinic_cases.reviewer_test: Evidence test: say which allowed change tries to alter the number, why the chosen account survives, and what conclusion that surviving account can actually force.

repair_clinic_cases.title: Quotient space as a square with arrows
repair_clinic_cases.flawed_explanation: A quotient space is shown by drawing a square with arrows on the sides.
repair_clinic_cases.why_it_fails: The sentence mistakes the code for the object. The arrows are not decoration on a square; they are instructions that decide which points become the same point in the finished space. If the reader reasons from the flat square after the rule has been applied, they may count boundaries or routes that no longer exist.
repair_clinic_cases.repair_move: State the identification rule before reasoning from the picture. Then say what route, boundary, or side behavior changes after the rule is applied. The repair should make the reader perform the gluing mentally before trusting any claim about the surface.
repair_clinic_cases.strong_version: A quotient-space drawing is a set of instructions. The square is only a readable way to say which edge points are identified. After the identifications are made, some apparent borders may disappear and the routes on the finished surface may differ from routes on the flat drawing. The mathematical object is the completed surface defined by the rule, not the ink before the rule is used.
repair_clinic_cases.reviewer_test: Evidence test: say which points are being declared identical, what apparent boundary changes after that declaration, and which claim would be wrong if the flat drawing were read literally.

repair_clinic_cases.title: Generic position as making the drawing nicer
repair_clinic_cases.flawed_explanation: Generic position means we move the picture slightly so it looks nicer and avoids special cases.
repair_clinic_cases.why_it_fails: This treats generic position as visual cleanup. The course uses the small move to create ordinary events that can be counted, signed, or isolated without hidden coincidences. Calling the picture nicer hides the permission question: the nudge must be legal and must preserve the feature the proof cares about.
repair_clinic_cases.repair_move: Say what accident is removed and what evidence becomes available afterward: clean crossings, separated events, isolated defects, or a defined sign rule. Then say why the nudge did not change the protected question.
repair_clinic_cases.strong_version: Generic position is a way to replace a fragile exact accident with an ordinary case that can carry evidence. After a tiny legal nudge, crossings can be separated, defects can be isolated, and signs or counts can be assigned. The cleaner picture earns trust only when its events can be audited and the nudge keeps the same object and the same question.
repair_clinic_cases.reviewer_test: Evidence test: identify the removed accident, the count or sign rule that becomes possible, and the reason the small move was legal for the original problem.

repair_clinic_cases.title: Fixed point as a point that does not move
repair_clinic_cases.flawed_explanation: A fixed point is a point that does not move, so fixed-point theorems tell us where something stays.
repair_clinic_cases.why_it_fails: The first phrase is only a start, and the second phrase is too strong. The course needs a rule from a space to itself, and the theorem often proves existence without locating the point. Saying does not move also blurs fixed points with equilibria unless the rule or field has been named.
repair_clinic_cases.repair_move: Name the domain, target, and rule, then translate the condition into self-agreement: the input and output are the same point in the same space. Then state the conclusion limit: the theorem may force at least one self-agreement point without telling where it is.
repair_clinic_cases.strong_version: A fixed point belongs to a rule that sends points of a space back into that same space. A point is fixed when the rule returns that exact point. The graph-and-diagonal picture turns this self-agreement into a meeting question, and a theorem may prove that some meeting exists without computing where it is, showing it is unique, or explaining a motion path.
repair_clinic_cases.reviewer_test: Evidence test: identify the rule, the space it maps into itself, the self-agreement condition, and the difference between existence, location, and uniqueness.

repair_clinic_cases.title: Index as the number of equilibria
repair_clinic_cases.flawed_explanation: The index counts how many equilibrium points a vector field has, so more equilibria means a larger index.
repair_clinic_cases.why_it_fails: This collapses a signed local account into a raw count. Index is assigned around an isolated defect by watching how arrows turn, and different defects can contribute different signed amounts. More dots do not automatically mean a larger total, because signs and turning behavior matter.
repair_clinic_cases.repair_move: Replace the raw count with the walk-around test. Say what loop encloses the defect and how arrows turn during one full circuit. Then distinguish the local index of one defect from the total index obtained by adding all defects on the same surface.
repair_clinic_cases.strong_version: Vector-field index is local signed evidence around one isolated defect. To read it, walk around a small loop containing that defect and watch how nearby arrows turn. Later, those local indices can be added and compared with a whole-surface number, but one index is not merely one equilibrium counted once. The evidence is the surrounding arrow pattern, not the label attached to the equilibrium.
repair_clinic_cases.reviewer_test: Evidence test: separate the number of defects from the signed turning account around each defect, and say when local indices may be added into one surface total.

repair_clinic_cases.title: Configuration space as a diagram of the machine
repair_clinic_cases.flawed_explanation: A configuration space is a picture of all the ways a machine can move.
repair_clinic_cases.why_it_fails: The sentence gestures in the right direction but stays too loose. A configuration space is not just a picture; one point must represent one complete allowed state, and forbidden states must be removed. Without that contract, a path in the diagram may pass through a physical impossibility or omit a real freedom.
repair_clinic_cases.repair_move: State what one point of the space represents, which freedoms vary, and which states are excluded before using topology to reason about motion. Then say what a path in the space means back in the original physical system.
repair_clinic_cases.strong_version: A configuration space records complete allowed states. For a moving system, one point might record every position or joint angle needed to describe the system at one instant. Collisions, blocked positions, or impossible choices must be removed, because paths in this space are supposed to represent real legal motions. The topological claim is only as honest as this translation between physical states and model points.
repair_clinic_cases.reviewer_test: Evidence test: say what one point represents, name at least one forbidden state that must not be included, and translate a path in the model back into real motion.

repair_clinic_cases.title: Poincare-Hopf as topology predicting motion
repair_clinic_cases.flawed_explanation: Poincare-Hopf says topology predicts how a dynamical system moves, so the theorem tells us the motion path.
repair_clinic_cases.why_it_fails: The sentence is too broad. The theorem compares the sum of local indices of isolated defects with the Euler characteristic of the same surface. It constrains defects; it does not solve the whole motion law. Predicts motion hides the exact conclusion and invites the reader to expect a trajectory.
repair_clinic_cases.repair_move: Name the surface, the vector field on that surface, every isolated defect, the local indices, and the Euler characteristic being compared. Then say what the theorem does not give: a solved path, a time evolution, or the exact location of every future state.
repair_clinic_cases.strong_version: Poincare-Hopf connects local failures of a vector field to the whole surface carrying that field. Each isolated defect has an index, and the sum of all those indices must match the Euler characteristic of the same surface. This can force defects or rule out some fields, but it does not compute every trajectory, describe how a particle moves between defects, or replace the differential equation with a full solution.
repair_clinic_cases.reviewer_test: Evidence test: include both sides of the contract, all local indices and the Euler characteristic of the same surface, and state the motion claim that remains unproved.

oral_exam_prompts.title: Explain the course in one chain
oral_exam_prompts.prompt: Explain the whole course as one chain, starting from a paper strip and ending with constraints on motion, without listing topic names as a substitute for reasons.
oral_exam_prompts.strong_answer: A complete response says the course begins by showing that small local views can miss whole-shape facts. The paper strip is not a throwaway surprise; it makes the reader ask what survives a full trip around the object. From there the course turns surprise into method: legal deformation lets a hard picture be replaced by an easier one, quotient rules build spaces from gluing instructions, protected counts turn change into evidence, signed intersections make meetings auditable, fixed points turn self-agreement into a forced meeting, vector-field index records local arrow failure, and configuration spaces let shape constrain motion. The chain has to sound like one growing habit: name the object, state the legal move, protect the fact that survives, and then say what the protected fact forces.
oral_exam_prompts.must_include: The answer must include a concrete early object, the allowed move that turns pictures into proof, one protected fact that travels through the course, and a later conclusion about forced meeting, forced defect, or blocked motion.
oral_exam_prompts.common_failure: A shallow response lists topics in order without saying why each topic is needed by the next one. It sounds organized but does not show how a paper-strip lesson becomes a method for proving later constraints.
oral_exam_prompts.follow_up: Where does the course first move from a visual surprise to a reusable proof method, what new obligation appears at that moment, and how does that obligation reappear in a late motion example?

oral_exam_prompts.title: Defend a deformation argument
oral_exam_prompts.prompt: Given a messy drawing, explain when simplifying it is a proof and when it changes the problem by breaking the allowed move.
oral_exam_prompts.strong_answer: A complete response treats simplification as valid only when every step is an allowed move for the original question. The easier endpoint is not evidence by itself; the legal route to it is the evidence. Name the starting object, the rulebook for motion, and the feature that must not change: endpoint order, obstacle avoidance, boundary behavior, gluing rule, side choice, crossing data, or state restriction. Also name a tempting illegal shortcut, such as cutting a loop, passing through a forbidden obstacle, moving a fixed endpoint, or changing the state space while pretending the same problem is still being solved.
oral_exam_prompts.must_include: The answer must name one allowed motion, one forbidden shortcut, the fact that survives the legal motion, and the exact moment where the shortcut would change the problem.
